title: Salary in Advance: How to Convert Your Hourly Rate to Annual Pay Under the National Minimum Wage or an Award
description: Learn how to convert hourly pay to annual salary using the 38-hour week, including National Minimum Wage, award rates, casual loading, super, and tax. Understand salary in advance
salarySummary: For a full-time employee working 38 hours per week, annual gross pay is hourly rate × 38 × 52, with super paid on top at 12% of ordinary earnings.

faqs.q: What is the difference between the National Minimum Wage and an award rate?
faqs.a: The National Minimum Wage from 1 July 2026 is $26.44 per hour for a 38-hour week, set by the Fair Work Commission. Award rates are minimum pay rates in specific industries or occupations, often higher than the national minimum wage. Most employees are covered by an award, which also includes penalty rates, allowances, and overtime rules. You can find the correct award rate using the Fair Work Ombudsman's pay guides.

faqs.q: How does casual loading affect my annual salary estimate?
faqs.a: Casual employees receive a 25% loading on top of the base hourly rate to compensate for not receiving paid leave. For example, the casual National Minimum Wage is $33.05 per hour. When converting to annual pay, the loading is included in the hourly rate before multiplying by hours and weeks. Our calculator has a checkbox to add 25% casual loading – do not enter a rate that already includes it.

faqs.q: What is a 'salary in advance' arrangement and how does it work?
faqs.a: A salary in advance (or annualised wage) is a fixed annual amount paid in equal instalments that covers minimum pay, penalties, overtime, allowances, and annual leave loading. It must be at least what the employee would have earned under the award for the year. The Fair Work Ombudsman requires employers to review the arrangement every 12 months and pay any shortfall. This is different from a simple salary contract that only covers the base rate.

bodyMarkdown:
## From Hourly to Annual: The Simple Formula

To estimate your annual gross pay from an hourly rate, multiply by the hours you work each week and then by 52 weeks. For a standard full-time role, we assume 38 hours per week – the ordinary hours under most awards and the National Minimum Wage. The formula is:

**Annual gross ≈ hourly rate × 38 × 52**

For example, at the National Minimum Wage of $26.44 per hour, the annual figure is about $52,270. A fortnightly pay would be roughly $2,010 (weekly × 2). This estimate assumes the same rate every week, no unpaid overtime, no penalty rates, no allowances, and no salary sacrifice. Superannuation is paid on top at 12% of ordinary earnings (up to the $270,830 maximum contribution base).

### National Minimum Wage vs Award Rates

The Fair Work Commission sets the National Minimum Wage each year. From 1 July 2026 it is $26.44 per hour for a 38-hour week, or $1,004.90 per week. This applies to award/agreement-free employees. However, most workers are covered by an industry or occupation award, which often has higher minimum rates. The Fair Work Ombudsman publishes pay guides for each award listing the correct minimum pay rates, allowances, and penalty rates. Always check your award before relying on the national minimum wage.

### Casual Loading

If you are a casual employee, you are entitled to a 25% loading on top of the base hourly rate. For the National Minimum Wage, that means $33.05 per hour. When using our [the timesheet](/) tool, tick the casual loading checkbox – never enter a rate that already includes the loading. The annual estimate will then reflect the higher casual rate.

## Understanding Salary in Advance

A **salary in advance** (also called an annualised wage) is a fixed annual amount paid in equal instalments that covers multiple entitlements in one go. Under some awards, an employer and employee can agree on an annualised wage that includes minimum pay, penalty rates, overtime, allowances, and annual leave loading. The Fair Work Ombudsman explains that the annualised wage must be at least what the employee would have earned under the award for the work performed.

This arrangement is different from a simple salary contract that only covers the base rate. With a salary in advance, the employer must review the arrangement every 12 months (or when employment ends) to ensure the employee hasn't been underpaid. If the actual entitlements exceed the annualised amount, the employer must pay the difference. Employers should also review the arrangement when award rates change or when the employee's working pattern shifts significantly.

### How It Affects Your Annual Estimate

If you are offered a salary in advance, your annual pay is already fixed – you don't need to convert an hourly rate. But if you are comparing an hourly offer to a salary offer, use our formula to see which is better. Remember that a salary in advance may include penalty rates and allowances, so it could be higher than a simple hourly × 38 × 52 calculation. Always check the written agreement to see what entitlements are covered.

## Tax and Super

From the annual gross figure, we estimate tax using the 2026–27 resident rates:
- Nil on the first $18,200
- 15% on income from $18,201 to $45,000
- 30% on income from $45,001 to $135,000
- 37% on income from $135,001 to $190,000
- 45% on income above $190,000

Plus the Medicare levy of 2% (using 2025–26 single reduction thresholds as 2026–27 thresholds were not confirmed). Superannuation is 12% of ordinary earnings, paid on top of your salary, and capped at the $270,830 maximum contribution base. This means if your annual gross exceeds that cap, super is calculated only on the first $270,830.

### Example: National Minimum Wage

- Hourly rate: $26.44
- Annual gross: $26.44 × 38 × 52 = $52,270 (rounded)
- Fortnightly gross: $2,010
- Super (12% on top): $6,272
- Estimated tax (including Medicare): about $7,300 (estimate only)
- Estimated take-home: about $44,970 per year

For a casual at $33.05/hour, annual gross is $65,330, super $7,840, and take-home around $51,600.

## Using Our Tools

Our [pay guides](/blog) page links to the Fair Work Ombudsman's official pay guides for your award. The [reference tables](/data) provide quick lookups for minimum wages and tax brackets. And of course, [the timesheet](/) lets you enter your base hourly rate, add casual loading, and see the annual, fortnightly, and weekly figures with tax and super estimates.

Remember: this is an estimate, not a determination of your pay or tax. Always consult your employer, a tax professional, or the Fair Work Ombudsman for your specific situation.
